summary: Defines the multipart/report MIME type, a container for email reports of any kind. Only its use for delivery status reports is specified here, but the aim is for all report types to share one format. It was replaced by RFC 3462.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of a folder that holds a short note plus the original letter that went wrong. This defines that kind of folder so mail programs know how to open error reports.

questions: how are mail bounce messages structured
subtitle: A standard MIME container for mail system reports such as delivery failure notices.

tldr.problem: Mail programs need to recognise automatically that a message is a mail system report, and handle it differently from ordinary mail.
tldr.mechanism: The Multipart/Report MIME type is a top-level container with two or three parts: a human-readable message, a machine-parsable description of the event, and optionally the returned original message.
tldr.outcome: This RFC defines the container for delivery status reports and a Text/RFC822-Headers type for returning only headers. It has been obsoleted by RFC 3462.

today: RFC 1892 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 3462, which is the specification to use now.

sections.title: The Multipart/Report Type
sections.content:
Multipart/Report is a general family or container type for electronic mail reports of any kind. This memo defines its use only for delivery status reports, but mail programs benefit if one content type is used for all kinds of reports.

It is MIME type multipart, subtype report, with the required parameters boundary and report-type. Its syntax is identical to Multipart/Mixed. When a report is sent, Multipart/Report must be the top-level content type of the message, so that an automatic processor can tell from the RFC 822 headers that it is a report. The report-type parameter names the MIME subtype of the second body part.
sections.plainLanguage: The report's outer wrapper is always labelled as a report, so a mail program can spot it at once.

sections.title: The Body Parts
sections.content:
A Multipart/Report contains two or three parts, in this order:

  • Part 1 (required): a human-readable message that describes what caused the report. It may use any MIME standards-track content type, charset or language, and Multipart/Alternative may be used for several languages.
  • Part 2 (required): a machine-parsable account of the reported event. The first such type, Message/delivery-status, is defined in RFC 1894.
  • Part 3 (optional): the returned message or a portion of it, to help human experts diagnose problems.

Returning content can waste bandwidth. Without an explicit request for a level of return, such as one made through RFC 1891, the agent generating the report should return the full message content.
sections.plainLanguage: The folder has a note for people, a form for machines, and sometimes a copy of the original letter.

sections.title: Text/RFC822-Headers and 7-Bit Paths
sections.content:
If non-7-bit data must be returned and the return path may not be 8-bit capable, the original message MAY be re-encoded into a legal 7-bit MIME message, or the Text/RFC822-Headers content type MAY be used to return only the original headers.

Text/RFC822-Headers labels the RFC 822 headers of a failed message. They are not the complete message and should not be returned as Message/RFC822. The part should contain all header lines, meaning everything before the first blank line, including the MIME-Version and MIME Content- headers. It needs no parameters, and 7-bit encoding is normally enough, though broken headers may use quoted-printable.
sections.plainLanguage: If the whole letter will not fit through a narrow pipe, you can send just the envelope information instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Using report types automatically without authentication causes problems. Forged negative reports can enable denial-of-service attacks when reports drive automated maintenance of directories or mailing lists. Forged positive reports may make a sender wrongly believe that a message was delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can fake a note saying a letter was lost or arrived, so a robot should not trust such notes blindly.
